original_question: For functions defined on a finite interval, what is the full characterization of one-parameter families of fractional integral operators I^alpha and associated fractional derivative operators D^alpha that satisfy the six desiderata HL1-HL6: linearity of I^alpha and D^alpha, the semigroup law I^alpha1 o I^alpha2 = I^(alpha1+alpha2), the left-inverse identity D^alpha o I^alpha = Id, existence of the limits D^alpha -> D^0 as alpha -> 0 and D^alpha -> D^1 as alpha -> 1, D^0 equal to the identity, and D^1 equal to the first derivative?
target_in_paper: Section 2.4, Open Problem 3: determine the general form of the fractional integrals and derivatives for functions on a finite interval in the sense of the desiderata from Sect. 2.1. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the finite-interval setting, the one-parameter families {I^alpha} and {D^alpha}, and the six desiderata HL1-HL6 as the governing conditions; it also correctly treats the problem as a joint characterization of fractional integrals and fractional derivatives rather than of only one side. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
missing_details: The paper normalizes the finite interval to [0,1] in Sect. 2.2 ('without loss of generality'), whereas your draft speaks only of an unspecified finite interval. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The order parameter is explicitly real and nonnegative, alpha >= 0, in Sect. 2.1; in the finite-interval discussion, D^0 is fixed by Remark 1 and the derivative theory is then mainly developed for 0 < alpha <= 1. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

HL1-HL6 are meant to hold on suitable nontrivial linear spaces of functions, not on all functions indiscriminately; Sect. 2.1 also states that the exact spaces and the precise sense of the limits in HL4 are not specified there and are referred to [30]. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

To make D^1 stand-alone and paper-faithful, one should say that the first derivative is interpreted on AC([0,1]) in the weak sense defined by formula (10). ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

The paper separates the surrounding program into Open Problem 1 (characterize admissible integrals), Open Problem 2 (characterize derivative families associated with the Riemann-Liouville integrals through the 1st Fundamental Theorem), and Open Problem 3 (deduce the general form of both); your draft jumps directly to the combined formulation. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

Theorem 1 gives uniqueness of the Riemann-Liouville integral family only under the stronger CM1-CM4 assumptions, so the official open problem is not already solved at the weaker HL1-HL6 level. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))

Sect. 2.2 stresses that there are infinitely many derivative families associated with the Riemann-Liouville integrals via the 1st Fundamental Theorem, including the Hilfer and nth-level families, so the refined question should not suggest an a priori unique derivative family. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
refined_question: On the finite interval [0,1] (the normalization adopted in Sect. 2.2), determine the general form of all one-parameter families of operators {I^alpha}_{alpha>=0} and {D^alpha}_{alpha>=0}, for real orders alpha >= 0, acting on suitable nontrivial linear spaces of functions, such that: (1) every I^alpha and D^alpha is linear; (2) I^{alpha1} o I^{alpha2} = I^{alpha1+alpha2} for all alpha1, alpha2 >= 0; (3) D^alpha o I^alpha = Id on the relevant common domain for every alpha >= 0; (4) the limits D^alpha -> D^0 as alpha -> 0 and D^alpha -> D^1 as alpha -> 1 exist in the operative sense of Sect. 2.1 and define linear maps; (5) D^0 = Id; and (6) D^1 coincides with the first-order derivative d/dx, understood on AC([0,1]) in the weak sense of formula (10). Equivalently, characterize the fractional integrals and derivatives for functions on a finite interval in the sense of desiderata (HL1)-(HL6). ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
justification: The draft most closely matches Section 2.4, Open Problem 3, because that is the paper's official request to deduce the general form of fractional integrals and derivatives on a finite interval 'in the sense of the desiderata' from Sect. 2.1. The nearby context needed to sharpen the question is as follows: Sect. 2.1 defines HL1-HL6 for real orders alpha >= 0; Sect. 2.2 then fixes [0,1] without loss of generality, identifies the Riemann-Liouville integral family as uniquely singled out by the stronger CM1-CM4 assumptions in Theorem 1, defines the first derivative via formula (10), proves uniqueness of the Riemann-Liouville derivative on I^alpha(L^1(0,1)) in Theorem 3, and also explains that infinitely many other derivative families associated with the Riemann-Liouville integrals exist, including Hilfer and nth-level families. This shows that your draft is very close in spirit, but it needed the paper's exact scope, order range, domain conventions, and function-space caveats to become fully stand-alone and paper-faithful. ([link.springer.com](https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s11071-021-07158-9.pdf))
